subject: chemistry
question_text: What is Le Chatelier's principle? Discuss briefly the factors which can influence the equilibrium.

steps.why: The one sentence names the three changes and states the single rule; the three paragraphs below are this sentence applied to each factor in turn.
common_mistakes: Writing that the system opposes or resists the change, as if it acted on purpose. State it literally: the equilibrium shifts in the direction that reduces the change.
Naming only one factor in the statement. Concentration, pressure and temperature all belong in it.
steps.memory_tip: One rule, three knobs: change something, and the shift goes the way that reduces that change.
steps.margin_note: One literal sentence. Each factor below is this rule applied once.

steps.label: Concentration
lines: of a reactant shifts the equilibrium in the
Increasing the concentration of a product
shifts it in the backward direction.
steps.why: Adding a substance raises its concentration; the shift that reduces this change is the one that uses that substance up — forward for an added reactant, backward for an added product.
common_mistakes: Writing that adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium backward. The shift consumes what was added, so it goes forward.
Forgetting the product half of the statement.
steps.memory_tip: The shift eats the added substance: add reactant, go forward; add product, go backward.
steps.margin_note: Both halves — added reactant and added product — carry this mark.

steps.label: Pressure
lines: Pressure: increasing the pressure shifts a
gaseous equilibrium towards the side with
the smaller number of gas moles.
Decreasing the pressure shifts it towards
the side with the larger number of gas
steps.why: Fewer gas moles occupy less volume and give a lower pressure, so moving to the smaller side is the shift that reduces a pressure increase.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the Δn = 0 exception, where pressure changes nothing.
Counting solids and liquids in the mole count. Only gaseous moles decide the shift.
steps.memory_tip: Higher pressure pushes the reaction to the smaller side — fewer gas moles, less volume.
steps.margin_note: Write the Δn = 0 exception; it is the detail this factor is marked on.

steps.label: Temperature

lines.text: Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction; lowering it shifts it in the exothermic direction

lines: A catalyst does not shift the equilibrium;
it only reduces the time needed to reach
steps.why: The endothermic direction absorbs the added heat, so it is the direction that reduces a temperature rise. The catalyst line closes the factor list: rate changes, position does not.
common_mistakes: Writing that heating always shifts the reaction forward. It shifts it in whichever direction is endothermic for that reaction.
Listing the catalyst as a factor that shifts the equilibrium. It does not; it changes only the time taken.
steps.memory_tip: Heat is treated like a substance: add heat, and the shift goes in the direction that absorbs heat.
steps.margin_note: The catalyst line is unmarked here but shows the factor list is complete.

insider_note: Write the principle as one sentence, then give each factor its own labelled paragraph — the examiner marks the three factors separately.
